﴿By the racers, panting,﴾ ﴿and the strikers of sparks,﴾ ﴿and the raiders at dawn,﴾ ﴿and stirrers up thereby of dust,﴾ ﴿and penetrating thereby into the midst of a company.﴾ ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful,﴾ ﴿and indeed, he is a witness to that,﴾ ﴿and indeed, he is intense in love of wealth.﴾

The description may also be applied to the running of a human being, and I think it is by way of comparison with horses. From this is the term 'addA' al-'Arab (the swift runners of the Arabs), who are four: al-Sulayk ibn al-Sulakah, al-Shanfara, Ta'abbata Sharran, and 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri. They are cited as a proverb for running.

The feminine form of this description here is because it is a description of things that do not reason.

Al-dabh (panting) is the agitation of breath that repeatedly moves in the throat without coming out of the mouth, and it is one of the sounds of horses and beasts of prey. 'Ata' reported: I heard Ibn 'Abbas describe the dabh: "ah ah."

And from Ibn 'Abbas: no animal pants except the horse, the dog and the fox. This is the statement of the people of language, and it is restricted to it in the Qamus. Ibn Jarir narrated with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas who said: While I was sitting in al-Hijr, a man came to me and asked me about ﴿the racers, panting﴾. I said to him: "The horses when they raid in the way of Allah, then they retire at night, and they prepare their food and kindle their fire." He turned away from me and went to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was beneath the water-drawing place of Zamzam, and asked him about it. He said: "Did you ask anyone about it before me?" He said: "Yes, I asked Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: The horses that raid in the way of Allah." He said: "Go and call him to me." When I stood at his head, he said: "You give fatwa to people about what you have no knowledge of. By Allah, the first raid in Islam was Badr, and there were with us only two horses: a horse for al-Zubayr and a horse for al-Miqdad. So how could they be 'the racers, panting'? Rather, 'the racers, panting' are the camels from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and from Muzdalifah to Mina." He meant by this that the surah is Meccan, before the beginning of the raids, the first of which was the battle of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So I withdrew from my statement and returned to what 'Ali had said."

There is nothing in the statement of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that clearly states that it is Meccan or Medinan. And like what 'Ali said, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim, Mujahid and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr also said.

Al-dabh is not applied to the sound of camels according to the people of language. If "al-'Adiyat" is taken to mean camels, al-Mubarrad and some of the people of language said: whoever makes it refer to camels makes "dabhan" mean "dab'an" (flank), it is said: the she-camel "dabahat" in her journey and "dab'at," when she extends her flanks in travel. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the horses "dabahat" and "dab'at" when they run, that is, when the horse extends its flanks while running. So dabh is a dialectal form of dab'; it is from the change of the 'ayn into ha'. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "it is not established." However, the author of the Qamus relied on it. And according to the interpretation of "al-'Adiyat" as camels, the dabh is borrowed for the sound of camels, i.e., from the intensity of running the repeated sounds in their throats grew strong until they resembled the panting of horses; or dabh is meant as dab' in the dialect of substitution.

"Dabhan" is in the accusative. It may be made a circumstantial qualifier of "al-'Adiyat" if what is meant is the sound that repeats in their bellies at the time of running; or it may be made to specify the type of running if its origin is "dabhan."

If it is taken that the one sworn by is the mounts of the pilgrimage, then the oath by them is to glorify them for what they help with in the rites of the Hajj. The oath by them was chosen because the listeners are certain that what is sworn upon by them is established, for they are glorified by all, from the polytheists and the Muslims.

Al-Muriyat: those that strike fire, i.e., kindle.

Al-qadh: the rubbing of one body against another to produce fire; it is said: "qadaha fa-awra" (he struck and kindled). "Qadhan" is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasizing its verb. Each of the hooves of horses and the pads of camels strikes sparks when they strike the flint stone, which is called the fire of al-Hubahib. Al-Shanfara, describing himself in running as a camel, said:

When the rough flinty ground meets my pads, there flies from it a spark and a shower of sparks.

This is a metaphor for going to the utmost in running and intensity of speed in travel.

It is possible that what is meant is the striking of fires at night when they stop for their needs and food. Here al-shahid may be in the sense of one who acknowledges, as in (ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah).

وهُوَ الرَّبُّ والشَّهِيدُ عَلى يَوْ ∗∗∗ مِ الخِيارَيْنِ والبَلاءُ بَلاءُ
"He is the Lord and the Witness over the day of the two choices, and the trial is a trial."

Al-shadid: the stingy one. Abu Dhu'ayb said in elegy:

"We guarded him with garments in the bottom of a pit, stingy over what the sand of the grave has gathered within the tomb."

Al-jawl, with fatha or damma, means dust, as it is also said of the stingy, the one who is excessively tight-fisted. Tarafah said:

عَقِيلَةُ مالِ الفاحِشِ المُتَشَدِّدِ
"The choicest property of the vile, tight-fisted one."

The lam in ﴿لِحُبِّ الخَيْرِ﴾ is the lam of causation, and al-khayr means wealth; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إنْ تَرَكَ خَيْرًا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180].

The meaning: indeed in the disposition of man is avarice because of his love of wealth, that is, of increasing it; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ومَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

The fronting of ﴿لِحُبِّ الخَيْرِ﴾ before its complement is for concern with the strangeness of this complement and for regard for the rhyme; and its fronting before its governing element, which is connected with the lam of initiation, which has precedence of position, is because it is a prepositional phrase, as you have learned in His saying: ﴿لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ﴾.

Love of wealth impels one to withhold kindness. The Arabs used to reproach one another with stinginess, yet they were, in the pre-Islamic era, stingy in comforting the poor and the weak, and they would devour the wealth of orphans; but they would squander wealth on displays of reputation, in drinking gatherings, and in gambling. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿ولا تَحُضُّونَ عَلى طَعامِ المِسْكِينِ﴾ [al-Fajr: 18] ﴿وتَأْكُلُونَ التُّراثَ أكْلًا لَمًّا﴾ [al-Fajr: 19] ﴿وتُحِبُّونَ المالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا﴾ [al-Fajr: 20]).

He turned away from me and went to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was beneath the water-drawing place of Zamzam, and asked him about it. He said: "Did you ask anyone about it before me?" He said: "Yes, I asked Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: The horses that raid in the way of Allah." He said: "Go and call him to me." When I stood at his head, he said: "You give fatwa to people about what you have no knowledge of. By Allah, the first raid in Islam was Badr, and there were with us only two horses: a horse for al-Zubayr and a horse for al-Miqdad. So how could they be 'the racers, panting'? Rather, 'the racers, panting' are the camels from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and from Muzdalifah to Mina." He meant by this that the surah is Meccan, before the beginning of the raids, the first of which was the battle of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So I withdrew from my statement and returned to what 'Ali had said."

There is nothing in the statement of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that clearly states that it is Meccan or Medinan. And like what 'Ali said, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim, Mujahid and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr also said.

Al-dabh is not applied to the sound of camels according to the people of language. If "al-'Adiyat" is taken to mean camels, al-Mubarrad and some of the people of language said: whoever makes it refer to camels makes "dabhan" mean "dab'an" (flank), it is said: the she-camel "dabahat" in her journey and "dab'at," when she extends her flanks in travel. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the horses "dabahat" and "dab'at" when they run, that is, when the horse extends its flanks while running. So dabh is a dialectal form of dab'; it is from the change of the 'ayn into ha'. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "it is not established." However, the author of the Qamus relied on it. And according to the interpretation of "al-'Adiyat" as camels, the dabh is borrowed for the sound of camels, i.e., from the intensity of running the repeated sounds in their throats grew strong until they resembled the panting of horses; or dabh is meant as dab' in the dialect of substitution.

"Dabhan" is in the accusative. It may be made a circumstantial qualifier of "al-'Adiyat" if what is meant is the sound that repeats in their bellies at the time of running; or it may be made to specify the type of running if its origin is "dabhan."

If it is taken that the one sworn by is the mounts of the pilgrimage, then the oath by them is to glorify them for what they help with in the rites of the Hajj. The oath by them was chosen because the listeners are certain that what is sworn upon by them is established, for they are glorified by all, from the polytheists and the Muslims.

Al-Muriyat: those that strike fire, i.e., kindle.

Al-qadh: the rubbing of one body against another to produce fire; it is said: "qadaha fa-awra" (he struck and kindled). "Qadhan" is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasizing its verb. Each of the hooves of horses and the pads of camels strikes sparks when they strike the flint stone, which is called the fire of al-Hubahib. Al-Shanfara, describing himself in running as a camel, said:

When the rough flinty ground meets my pads, there flies from it a spark and a shower of sparks.

This is a metaphor for going to the utmost in running and intensity of speed in travel.

It is possible that what is meant is the striking of fires at night when they stop for their needs and food. It is also permitted that ﴿the strikers of sparks﴾ is a metaphor for the kindling of war, because war is compared to fire. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. Then "qadhan" would be an intensifying complement of the metaphor "al-Muriyat" and in the accusative as an absolute object of "al-Muriyat." It is also permitted that "qadhan" means extracting broth from the cooking pot into cups to feed the army or the riders, and it is derived from the noun qadah, which is a dish; then "qadhan" would be a verbal noun in the accusative as an object of purpose.

Al-Mughirat: an active participle from aghara; and al-igharah is applied to an army's raiding of a dwelling, which is its most famous usage. The attribution of the raid to the pronoun of "al-'Adiyat" is a rational metaphor, for those who raid are its riders; but the horses or the camels of the raid are causes and means of the raid.

And al-igharah is also applied to rushing in travel.

"Subhan" is an adverb of time. If "al-Mughirat" is interpreted as the horses of the raiders, then restricting this to the time of dawn is because when they raided, they would not attack a people except after dawn; for this reason the warner of a tribe, when he warned his people of the coming of the enemy, would cry: "Ya sabahah!" Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But when it descends upon their courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat: 177].

If "al-Mughirat" is interpreted as the swiftly moving camels, then what is meant is their pushing from Muzdalifah to Mina at the morning of the day of sacrifice, and they used to push off early when the sun rose over Thabir; and among their sayings about that: "Shine, O Thabir, so that we may raid."

Narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili with a weak chain of transmission, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The kanud is the one who eats alone, withholds his gift (rifd), and beats his servant." This is an explanation of the lowest meanings of kanud, for eating alone, that is, not feeding anyone with him, or not feeding the needy, is a neglect of some degrees of gratitude for the blessing; likewise withholding the gift (rifd); and similarly beating his servant, for in it there is forgetting the gratitude owed to Allah who made the servant a possession of his and did not make him a possession of the servant. Thus it indicates that what is more severe than this is more deserving of the description of kanud.

It has been said: the definite article in (al-insan) is for a known reference (al-'ahd), and that what is meant by it is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. It has also been said: it is Qirtah ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn Nawfal al-Qurashi.

The lam in (li-rabbihi) is the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah), because kanud is a descriptive noun that does not act as a primary verb, and it relates to its objects only by resemblance to the verb in derivation; therefore it is common for its object to be joined by the lam of reinforcement, and for it to be placed after its object.

The fronting of (li-rabbihi) serves to express concern with what this kanud relates to, in order to make this ingratitude more shameful, in that it is directed toward the Lord, who is the most deserving of all existents of gratitude; and the greatest of this is the polytheism of the polytheists. For this reason the statement is emphasized with the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') that enters upon the predicate of (inna), to express wonder at this report.

The fronting of (li-rabbihi) before its governing element, which is connected with the lam of initiation, and the lam is among those that have precedence of position (min dhawat al-sadr); for they allow wide latitude with prepositional phrases and adverbial expressions. Ibn Hisham holds that the lam of initiation occurring in the predicate of (inna) does not have precedence of position.

The pronoun in ﴿وإنَّهُ عَلى ذَلِكَ لَشَهِيدٌ﴾ refers to al-insan according to the apparent sense required by the coherence of pronouns and the unity of the subject spoken of, and this is the view of the majority.

Al-shahid is applied to the witness, who is one who reports what confirms the claim of a claimant; it is applied to the present one; and from this comes its application to the knowing one from whom no known thing escapes; and it is applied to one who acknowledges, because he bears witness against himself.

Here al-shahid may be in the sense of one who acknowledges, as in (ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah).

The meaning: man acknowledges his ingratitude toward his Lord without intending to acknowledge it, and this occurs in slips of speech, like the statement of the polytheists about their idols: ﴿ما نَعْبُدُهم إلّا لِيُقَرِّبُونا إلى اللَّهِ زُلْفى﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. This is a statement that entails their admission that they worshipped what does not deserve to be worshipped, and associated with the One who deserves to be singled out in worship; is this not ingratitude toward their Lord? Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وشَهِدُوا عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ أنَّهم كانُوا كافِرِينَ﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. And it also occurs in slips of action, as it happens to the Muslim in acts of disobedience.

The purpose of this sentence is to make the ingratitude of man appear shameful, in that it is known to its possessor by even slight reflection upon his sayings and deeds. Accordingly, the preposition (ala) is connected with (shahid), and the demonstrative refers to the ingratitude derived from the attribute (kanud).

It is also permissible that (shahid) means (knowing, 'alim), like the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza concerning 'Amr ibn Hind:

وهُوَ الرَّبُّ والشَّهِيدُ عَلى يَوْ ∗∗∗ مِ الخِيارَيْنِ والبَلاءُ بَلاءُ
"He is the Lord and the Witness over the day of the two choices, and the trial is a trial."

The complement of (shahid) is omitted, indicated by the context, meaning: he knows that Allah is his Lord, that is, by the proofs of lordship; and his saying (ala dhalika) would mean: along with that, that is, along with that ingratitude he knows that He is his Lord, deserving of gratitude and obedience, not of ingratitude. Thus the preposition (ala) is in the sense of (ma'a, with), like His saying: ﴿وآتى المالَ عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] and ﴿ويُطْعِمُونَ الطَّعامَ عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ [al-Insan: 8], and the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

فَبَقِينا عَلى الشَّناءَةِ تَنْمِي ∗∗∗ نا حُصُونٌ وعِزَّةٌ قَعْساءُ
"So we remained, with enmity, while fortresses and a steadfast might nurtured us."

The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and this is an added intensification of the wonder at the ingratitude of man.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sufyan said: the pronoun in (wa-innahu) refers to (rabbihi), that is, and indeed Allah is witness over that; the meaning is that Allah knows that within man's soul, and this is an allusion warning of the reckoning for it. This is supported by the fact that the pronoun refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun, and both views were reported from Mujahid and Qatadah, so perhaps they regarded both interpretations as permissible, and this is preferable.

The fronting of (ala dhalika) before (shahid) is for concern, wonder, and regard for the rhyme (fasilah).

Al-shadid: the stingy one. Abu Dhu'ayb said in elegy:

حَذَرْناهُ بِأثْوابٍ في قَعْرِ هُوَّةٍ ∗∗∗ شَدِيدٍ عَلى ما ضَمَّ في اللَّحْدِ جُولُها
"We guarded him with garments in the bottom of a pit, stingy over what the sand of the grave has gathered within the tomb."

Al-jawl, with fatha or damma, means dust, as it is also said of the stingy, the one who is excessively tight-fisted. Tarafah said:

عَقِيلَةُ مالِ الفاحِشِ المُتَشَدِّدِ
"The choicest property of the vile, tight-fisted one."

The lam in ﴿لِحُبِّ الخَيْرِ﴾ is the lam of causation, and al-khayr means wealth; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إنْ تَرَكَ خَيْرًا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180].

The meaning: indeed in the disposition of man is avarice because of his love of wealth, that is, of increasing it; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ومَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

The fronting of ﴿لِحُبِّ الخَيْرِ﴾ before its complement is for concern with the strangeness of this complement and for regard for the rhyme; and its fronting before its governing element, which is connected with the lam of initiation, which has precedence of position, is because it is a prepositional phrase, as you have learned in His saying: ﴿لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ﴾.

Love of wealth impels one to withhold kindness. The Arabs used to reproach one another with stinginess, yet they were, in the pre-Islamic era, stingy in comforting the poor and the weak, and they would devour the wealth of orphans; but they would squander wealth on displays of reputation, in drinking gatherings, and in gambling. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿ولا تَحُضُّونَ عَلى طَعامِ المِسْكِينِ﴾ [al-Fajr: 18] ﴿وتَأْكُلُونَ التُّراثَ أكْلًا لَمًّا﴾ [al-Fajr: 19] ﴿وتُحِبُّونَ المالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا﴾ [al-Fajr: 20]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 100, verses 9–10:

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾ ﴿and what is in the breasts is made known?﴾

The interrogative of denunciation (istifham inkari) is placed as a consequence of the report of man's ingratitude (kunud) and miserliness (shuhh): it denounces man's lack of knowledge of the time when what is in the graves is scattered forth and what is in the breasts is brought to light, for it is a strange matter how man could be heedless of it. The interrogative hamza has been placed before the fa' of the conjunction (fa' al-ta'rif), because the interrogative has the front position in speech (sadr al-kalam).

(Idha) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyya) governing the omitted object of (ya'lamu) by way of restriction (iqtisar), so that the listener may go in estimating it every possible direction, for the purpose of instilling awe (tahwil).

The meaning is: Does he not know the punishment as a recompense for him for what is in his ingratitude and his stinginess of a wrongdoing varying in degree, to the extent of making eternal abiding in the Fire obligatory?

Both objects of (ya'lamu) have been omitted, and there is no indication in the wording that specifies their estimation; the listener is left to estimate what the context requires of threat and awe. This omission is called by the grammarians al-hadhf al-iqtisari (omission by restriction). Omitting both objects by restriction is permissible according to the majority of grammarians, and this is the verified view, although Sibawayh prohibits it.

Bu'thira: its meaning is "turned over from the bottom to the top," and what is meant by it is the revival of what is in the graves of the dead, with their bodies complete or parts of them. Its explanation has preceded at His words, exalted is He: ﴿When the graves are scattered forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 4] in Surat al-Infitar.

Hussila: it was gathered and counted. "What is in the breasts" is what is in the souls of inner thoughts (dama'ir) and characters (akhlaq), that is: their tally is gathered and they are reckoned for.

﴿Indeed, their Lord is fully Aware of them that Day.﴾

This clause is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*, a new sentence that answers an implied question arising from the preceding denial). The meaning is: it would have been fitting for them to know that God observes them when what is in the graves is scattered and brought out, and to remember Him, because behind them lies a meticulous reckoning. This clause carries the function of a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*, a closing statement that generalizes the point just made).

His saying "that Day" (*yawma'idhin*) is connected to His saying "Aware" (*lakhabir*), meaning "All-Knowing."

"The Aware" (*al-Khabir*) is a metonymy for the One who recompenses with punishment and reward, as indicated by the restriction of it to "that Day." God's knowledge of them has been present since the life of this world. What is meant by His knowledge of them on the Day the graves are overturned is the knowledge upon which the requital is based.

Placing "them" (*bihim*) before its governing element, which is "Aware" (*lakhabir*), serves to emphasize it, so that they know that they are the intended object of this. Placing the prepositional phrase before the governing element when it is accompanied by the initial *lam* (*lam al-ibtida'*) is permissible, though the *lam* normally has the front position, because of the latitude in the usage of prepositional phrases and adverbials, as was mentioned just before in His saying ﴿Surely to his Lord he is ungrateful﴾ (Al-'Adiyat: 6), His saying ﴿and surely he is witness to that﴾ (Al-'Adiyat: 7), and His saying ﴿and surely he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ (Al-'Adiyat: 8). You have already learned that Ibn Hisham disputes the obligation of placing the *lam* of beginning, which occurs in the predicate of *inna*, at the front.

Surah Al-Qari'ah

The codices (*masahif*), the books of *tafsir* (Qur'anic exegesis), and the books of *sunnah* (prophetic tradition) all agree on naming this surah "Surat al-Qari'ah" (The Striking Calamity). Nothing has been transmitted about its naming from the words of the Companions (*sahabah*, the Prophet's companions) or the Successors (*tabi'un*, the generation after the Companions).

It is agreed that it is Meccan.

It is counted as the thirtieth in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat Quraysh and before Surat al-Qiyamah.

Its number of verses is ten according to the count of the people of Medina and the people of Mecca, eight according to the count of the people of Syria and Basra, and eleven according to the count of the people of Kufa.

* * *

It contains an affirmation of the occurrence of the Resurrection (*al-ba'th*) and of the terrors that precede it.

It also affirms the recompense for deeds: that the people of righteous deeds that are esteemed in the sight of God will be in bliss, and the people of evil deeds, which have no weight in God's sight, will be in the depths of the Blazing Fire.
